extra_misconceptions.fact: Squeezing a tick's body injects infectious fluids into the bite; grasp it close to the skin with fine-tipped tweezers and pull upward.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Grabbing an embedded tick by its swollen body with bare fingers is the fastest way to remove it safely.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Urban environments pose traffic hazards, broken glass, and sharp metal edges that still require a buddy pair and a pocket first aid kit.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Urban geocaches located in parking lots eliminate the need for a buddy system or basic first aid supplies.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Urushiol binds to skin proteins within minutes, so immediate washing with soap, cold water, and friction is required to prevent a rash.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing alcohol neutralizes urushiol oil on skin even several hours after brushing against poison ivy leaves.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Intact skin over a blister provides a sterile barrier against bacteria; cover it with a moleskin doughnut pad to relieve pressure.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Popping a friction blister on the trail with an unsterilized pocketknife speeds up skin recovery during a hike.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to reach blindly into a hollow log or rock crevice when searching for a hidden container?
What happens to your situational awareness when you stare continuously at a GPS screen while walking on uneven terrain?
Which physical indicator distinguishes life-threatening heatstroke from heat exhaustion during a summer cache hunt?
Under what condition does a minor heel hot spot turn into a debilitating blister if left untreated on the trail?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Geocaching rules strictly prohibit burying caches because digging destroys vegetation, accelerates soil erosion, and damages park property.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Burying a geocache under a few inches of soil is permitted as long as the cache page includes a shovel attribute.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Food and scented items attract rodents and bears that chew through plastic containers and become habituated to human food sources.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Placing wrapped candy or scented soap inside a forest geocache rewards finders without affecting local wildlife.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Proper geocaching etiquette requires trading even or trading up so the container remains rewarding for future finders.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Taking a high-value trade item from a cache without leaving an item of equal or greater value is standard practice.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every physical geocache placement requires explicit permission from the landowner or park agency before submitting the listing for review.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Public parkland is open to everyone, so hiding a physical cache container never requires permission from the land manager.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to fragile root systems and topsoil when dozens of geocachers dig around a buried container?
Where should a Scout position a cache relative to an established trail to prevent creating destructive social trails?
What steps must a cache owner complete when dismantling and archiving a retired geocache listing?
Why is it important to observe nearby bystanders before retrieving or re-hiding a container in a public park?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Trackables are game pieces with unique codes meant to move from cache to cache toward a stated goal, never kept as personal trade items.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Travel Bugs and collectible geocoins with tracking codes are SWAG prizes meant to be kept permanently in a personal collection.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Difficulty measures the mental challenge of solving or spotting the hide, whereas the terrain rating indicates physical travel demands.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A 5-star difficulty rating means the hike to the cache requires rock climbing gear, a boat, or scuba equipment.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Traditional caches sit at the posted coordinates, while Multi and Puzzle caches require solving stages or clues for the final location.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Multi-caches and Mystery or Puzzle caches always have the physical container hidden at the posted header coordinates.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Micro and nano caches hold only a tiny rolled logsheet, requiring geocachers to bring their own pen or pencil to sign the log.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Micro and nano containers are large enough to hold full-sized notebooks, pencils, and multiple trade items.

extra_socratic_questions: What distinguishes a trackable item like a Travel Bug from standard SWAG trinkets found inside a cache container?
Under what condition does a geocache receive a 5-star terrain rating even if the difficulty rating is only 1 star?
Which physical indicator on a cache page warns you whether dogs, bicycles, or winter access are allowed at the site?
Why does logging a Did Not Find (DNF) entry help both the cache owner and the next geocacher who searches the area?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Standard GPS receivers are passive listeners that calculate position by measuring time delays of radio signals broadcast from satellites.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Handheld GPS receivers transmit radio signals upward to orbiting satellites so the satellites can track the user.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Mismatched coordinate formats or datums shift the plotted waypoint by hundreds of meters or several miles from the actual target.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Entering coordinates in the wrong datum or format still guides you within ten feet of the intended waypoint.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Without a triaxial magnetic sensor, a GPS unit calculates heading from movement between points and spins randomly when you stop walking.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The electronic pointer arrow on a standard non-compass GPS receiver stays accurate even when you stand completely still.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Atmospheric interference, dense foliage, and steep canyon walls limit consumer GPS accuracy to roughly ten to thirty feet.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Consumer GPS units pinpoint a geocache to the exact inch regardless of overhead tree canopy or canyon walls.

extra_socratic_questions: Why must a GPS receiver lock onto at least four satellites to calculate both three-dimensional position and elevation?
What happens to your target location if you enter WGS 84 Degrees and Decimal Minutes into a unit set to Decimal Degrees?
Which environmental obstacles cause multipath signal reflection and degrade coordinate accuracy in the field?
What measurement confirms your GPS receiver has settled enough to average and mark a reliable new waypoint?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Batteries drain rapidly in cold weather and screens shatter on rocks, making a non-powered map and compass essential backup tools.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Carrying a fully charged smartphone or GPS receiver makes a paper topographic map and magnetic compass obsolete.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A straight-line GPS pointer ignores terrain obstacles like cliffs, deep streams, and private property that a topographic map clearly shows.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Following the straight-line bearing on a GPS screen always provides the safest and fastest route to a geocache.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Closely packed contour lines represent steep elevation changes or cliffs, while widely spaced lines indicate gentle slopes or flat ground.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Closely spaced contour lines on a topographic map indicate a flat, easy meadow suitable for rapid off-trail travel.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A compass needle aligns with local magnetic north, requiring declination adjustment to match the true north grid lines on a map.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A magnetic compass needle points directly toward true geographic north on every USGS topographic quadrangle.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to follow a straight-line GPS Go-To arrow without checking contour lines on a topographic map?
What happens to your compass bearing if you fail to adjust for local magnetic declination over a two-mile hike?
Which topographic map features reveal impassable cliffs, rivers, or swamps that a basic GPS waypoint arrow omits?
Under what condition does a magnetic baseplate compass outperform an electronic GPS receiver in backcountry terrain?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Official geocaching rules require signing the physical logbook inside the container before logging a Found It entry online.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Signing only the online cache page counts as an official find even if you skip signing the physical paper logbook.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Satellite drift makes the final twenty to thirty feet imprecise, so you must stop watching the screen and search likely hiding spots visually.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Walking with your eyes glued to the GPS distance counter until it reads zero feet is the best way to spot a cache.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Moving a cache ruins the owner's coordinates and hint; always return the container to the exact spot and cover it as you found it.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Moving a found geocache to an easier spot helps the next seeker and improves the overall quality of the hide.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A manually marked waypoint defaults to a sequential number, so you must edit the name and symbol yourself to identify it later.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Saving a waypoint on a GPS unit automatically names it with the official GC code and difficulty rating from the website.

extra_socratic_questions: At what distance from Ground Zero should you put away the GPS screen and rely on your eyes and geocaching sense?
Why should you record a new waypoint at your trailhead parking spot before hiking out to search for your first cache?
What happens to a geocache's survival rate if you fail to return the container to its exact original position and camouflage?
Which details should you include or omit when signing the physical paper logbook and posting your online Found It log?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Multiple consecutive Did Not Find logs or a disabled status usually mean the container is missing or damaged, so check recent logs first.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Every geocache listed on the map is ready to be found, even if the last five online logs are Did Not Find entries.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Spoiler photos ruin the search challenge for future finders and violate etiquette unless the cache owner explicitly requests a photo.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Posting a photo of the exact hiding spot and open container in your online log is helpful to the geocaching community.

extra_misconceptions.fact: ROT13 simply shifts each letter thirteen places in the alphabet, allowing anyone to decode the hint by hand using the key on the page.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Decoding an encrypted ROT13 hint on a cache printout requires a paid subscription or a special electronic decoder.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Beginners succeed far more often by selecting a recently found Traditional cache with low difficulty, low terrain, and a regular container.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Picking a high-difficulty micro cache for your very first search is the easiest way to complete Requirement 7.

extra_socratic_questions: Which clues in the recent activity logs tell you whether a local geocache is currently active or likely missing?
Why does the ROT13 substitution cipher protect the encrypted hint on a cache listing until you choose to decode it?
What information on the cache page helps you choose an appropriate first target from three local listings?
Why is parent or guardian permission required before creating an account or searching local caches on Geocaching.com?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cache owners must monitor online logs, replace soaked logbooks, repair broken containers, and maintain the site for as long as it is active.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hiding a new public geocache is a one-time task that requires no follow-up once the volunteer reviewer publishes the page.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Geocaching placement guidelines require at least 0.1 miles (528 feet) between physical caches to prevent saturation and searcher confusion.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Physical geocaches can be hidden twenty feet apart as long as they belong to different cache owners or different series.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A Travel Bug must be activated online with a stated mission and attached to a Hitchhiker object before finders can log its movements.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Releasing a Scouting Travel Bug into a cache without registering or activating its tracking code online lets you track its miles.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cache In Trash Out is both a formal community event type and an everyday habit of carrying a trash bag to clean litter on every cache hunt.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cache In Trash Out (CITO) applies only to organized annual cleanup events rather than everyday solo geocaching outings.

extra_socratic_questions: What details on a Cache to Eagle listing educate visiting geocachers about the Eagle Scout service project at that site?
What minimum distance must separate a new physical geocache from any existing physical cache stage during placement?
Which ongoing maintenance duties must a Scout perform during the three months after publishing a new public geocache?
What safety and scoring procedures are needed when setting up a multi-team GeoHunt or Cache In Trash Out service event?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Basic GPS units calculate heading from movement between satellite fixes, so players must walk several steps to orient the arrow.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A basic handheld GPS receiver points its directional arrow toward the next waypoint even when the player stands completely still.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Initial satellite locks have wide position error; letting the receiver settle or average readings for two minutes tightens accuracy.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Marking a course waypoint the instant the GPS unit acquires its first satellite fix gives players the most accurate coordinates.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Metal roofs and indoor walls block or bounce microwave satellite signals, causing severe multipath drift that confuses youth players.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hiding geohunt containers inside buildings or under metal pavilion roofs works well because GPS signals penetrate solid structures.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Public listing sites require permanent caches maintained for at least three months; temporary group geohunts use printed sheets only.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Temporary waypoints set up for a one-day troop or pack geohunt should be submitted for publication on public geocaching websites.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to player navigation when two geohunt waypoints sit closer together than the GPS unit's 20-foot accuracy margin?
Under what condition will entering identical waypoint coordinates on two GPS units send teams to spots 200 meters apart?
What measurement on the satellite status screen confirms you have waited long enough before saving a new course waypoint?
Why is it dangerous to let novice players walk toward a waypoint while staring continuously at the GPS compass arrow?
